deed: Robert Furchgott discovered that nitric oxide is a transient chemical signal in mammalian body cells
title: Robert Furchgott discovered that blood vessel cells release a substance that widens them: nitric oxide

trailer.text: Robert Furchgott was an American pharmacologist who was awarded the Nobel Prize together with Louis Ignarro and Ferid Murad.
In the 1950s he developed a method that tests, using a rabbit's artery, how blood vessels respond to medications, neurotransmitters and hormones.
In 1980 he showed that when the inner cell layer of blood vessels, the endothelium, is removed, acetylcholine no longer makes them relax and widen.
From this he concluded that a substance that causes expansion is formed in this layer.
In 1986 he and Ignarro, each separately, showed that the substance is nitric oxide, and the discovery made possible new medications for heart and cardiovascular diseases and for impotence.

stations.title: A boy from Charleston who wanted to be a scientist

paragraphs.text: Furchgott was born in Charleston, South Carolina, where his family ran a department store.
According to him, the store was started by his grandfather and was run by his father and his father's two brothers.
According to him, the store did not survive the Great Depression.
As a child he was an avid shell collector and watched birds, he recounted.
He received a bachelor's degree in chemistry from the University of North Carolina in 1937.
In 1940 he received a doctorate in biochemistry from Northwestern University in Illinois.

stations.title: A rabbit's artery and a strange response

paragraphs.text: He recounted that the experiments testing VEM and VDM were failures.
According to him, these failures tempered his enthusiasm and that of Zweifach.
In hindsight, Furchgott suggested that the substance VDM might be related to nitric oxide.
In the 1950s Furchgott developed a method for testing, using a rabbit's artery, how blood vessels respond to medications, neurotransmitters and hormones.
He recounted that a helical strip from a rabbit's aorta, properly cut and mounted, contracted again and again in the same way to epinephrine and norepinephrine.
But to acetylcholine the strips responded only by contracting.
This was the opposite of the expected response, because in the living body acetylcholine is known as a substance that strongly dilates blood vessels.
Only years later did he understand what had happened, he recounted: his method of preparing the strips had inadvertently removed all the endothelial cells.
In 1956 Furchgott joined the department of pharmacology at SUNY in Brooklyn.
Before that he was an assistant professor of pharmacology at the School of Medicine of Washington University in St. Louis, from 1949 to 1956.
In Brooklyn, from 1978, he focused on an anomalous response of preparations from rabbit aorta.
Sometimes they relaxed instead of contracting, as expected.
Furchgott also described the relaxation of aortic strips by light as an accidental discovery that arose from an observation in one experiment.
According to him, Matsunaga showed that the relaxation by light was enhanced because the light caused the release of NO from nitrite.
According to him, about 23 years after he moved to Brooklyn, his research dealt mainly with endothelium-dependent relaxation of blood vessels.

stations.title: The substance that comes from the lining of blood vessels

paragraphs.text: In 1980 Furchgott showed that when the endothelium is removed, acetylcholine no longer makes the blood vessel relax and widen.
He concluded that a substance that causes expansion is formed in this layer.
He recounted that he showed that the relaxation of arteries by acetylcholine is endothelium-dependent.
He named the not-yet-identified molecule EDRF.
It signals the smooth muscle cells in the blood vessel wall to relax and expand.
The relaxation resulted from the unexpected release of a factor from the cells of the inner lining, the endothelial cells.
According to The Washington Post, this recognition was a key step in what has been called the "nitric oxide revolution".

stations.title: A note written on an airplane: it is nitric oxide

paragraphs.text: According to Robert Wong, chairman of the department, a note from 1986 is the first record of Furchgott's hypothesis that the substance might be nitric oxide.
The department library at Downstate displays a note that Furchgott handwrote on the subject while he was on an airplane.
In 1986 Furchgott and Louis Ignarro, each separately, showed that the substance is nitric oxide, NO.
According to Furchgott, that year EDRF was identified as nitric oxide.
The two first announced their findings at a scientific conference in 1986, and triggered a wave of international research on nitric oxide.
Furchgott's work was linked with research by Ferid Murad from 1977.
Murad showed that nitroglycerin and related heart drugs induce the formation of nitric oxide.

stations.title: From a polluting gas to a signal in the body

paragraphs.text: According to The New York Times, the research proved that nitric oxide, known as an air pollutant, is also an important signal in the cardiovascular system.
According to the newspaper, it mediates blood pressure and blood flow.
According to Britannica, the work of the three uncovered an entirely new mechanism by which blood vessels in the body relax and widen.
Scientists later showed that many kinds of cells in the body manufacture nitric oxide, and that it helps regulate various body functions.
According to Encyclopedia.com, wider roles have been identified for it, including defense against infection and control of blood pressure.
The discovery made possible new medications, such as medications for heart and cardiovascular diseases and for impotence.
According to Britannica, the research of Murad, Furchgott and Ignarro was key to the development of Viagra, sildenafil citrate.
The Pfizer company called the discovery "a small piece of information" on the way to inventing the drug.
The discovery also suggested new therapies for high blood pressure and heart disease.
Researchers suggested that nitric oxide could be a key to improved treatments for heart disease, shock and cancer.
The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 1998 was awarded jointly to Robert Furchgott, Louis Ignarro and Ferid Murad.
The prize was given for discoveries concerning nitric oxide as a signalling molecule in the cardiovascular system.
The Swedish Nobel Assembly praised them for providing the first proof that a gas can perform important biochemical functions in the body.
According to The Washington Post, the laureates showed skeptical colleagues that a gas considered unstable can send important signals to vital organs.
A specialist said at the time of the announcement that this was a marvelously simple and creative story of a senior scientist at work in his laboratory.
Before that, Furchgott received the Gairdner Award in 1991.
In 1996 he received the Lasker Award for basic medical research.
The obituary in the journal Nature described him as a Nobel laureate who pioneered research into nitric oxide.
According to the SUNY Downstate website, Furchgott won the 1998 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, jointly with Louis Ignarro and Ferid Murad.
Furchgott and his wife Lenore had three daughters.
Both of Furchgott's wives died before him.
He was survived by three daughters, four grandchildren and a great-grandchild.
Furchgott died on May 19, 2009, in Seattle.
He died at the University of Washington Medical Center in Seattle, and no cause of death was reported.
According to the newspaper, his daughter Susan Furchgott confirmed his death.
